messages.content: We’re looking for partners looking to develop cutting edge open source silicon with us, we’d like to do some codevelopment on our 10 purchased wafer.space slots
What is the definition of "cutting edge" here? What exactly do you need?

Analog characterization chip 
gigabit ethernet 
PCIE (any gen)
Voltage regulators

are top line items
I can make you a linear regulator, but I don’t think the rest of those are possible
Well, analog characterization depends on *what* you want to characterize

All on a mature node of the late 1990s? You could have landed that money on a full GF180 MPW shuttle, if considering the minimum price you could have paid (~$20000, for 10x 0p5x0p5 bare die at early bird, which isn't even possible as there are just 9 of those), but you instead chose to buy 10 wafer.space slots where, even if you purchased at least a full slot, that 12.92mm^2 of silicon wouldn't handle most of the stuff mentioned. Other than potentially the linear voltage regulator Tholin mentioned.
we’ve already invested the funds, and we have enough conviction to bet on something risky like this
if it works, new possibilities on a mature 1990s node become possible
we aren’t paying for engineering time, but we’re giving people a free shot at trying something risky, and if even 2/10 chips work, it’ll be a great success
The physics may disagree, sadly. Specifically transistor gate delays, and use of aluminium wire interconnects for the 5 metal layers.
It might be "giving people a free shot" in your perspective, but judging the "cutting edge tech" expected, it's still focus on a limited talent pool.
100Mbit ethernet is in the spirit of the mission
if you think these limits are too far out, then what do you think is possible? you of course have seen the 8086 demo scene
the difference is that compiling code is free. well, we are making compiling silicon free
The 8086 demo scene was amazing because developers accepted the unforgiving hardware limits and optimised within them. They didn't try to force an 8086 MPU to render Crysis.
Great, let's do that with GF180 then! DeepAI is looking for collaborators, chip designers, we're giving away 3 Run 3 slots in hope of pushing the boundaries of open source!
I see! You donated one to Hack Club, right?
I appreciate that gesture!
That's us!
Even if you got those high speed interfaces on a gf180 chip, there is nothing you can put on that chip to generate or process data at those speeds.

WCH makes a chip that is a PCIe to RS232 adapter (just a PCIe version of their popular USBTTL chips). If you put that on a board with a gf180mcu SoC and set it to one of the higher supported UART rates, i.e. 500000bps, you’d have all the throughput you need.

To share my personal experience: I taped out a RISC-V core on GFMPW-1, about as performant as a non-pipelined core could get, and wired it up to a SPI <-> 10/100mbps ethernet bridge (enc28j60) and the system kept dropping packets because the RISC-V CPU struggled to process them faster than they were coming in.
Like, it’d frequently die during IPv6 SLAAC or IPv4 DHCP because the broadcast responses combined with background broadcast traffic on my home network overflowed the buffer.
So, 10/100mbps ethernet on gf180mcu would make sense, but then you’re hitting data processing speed limits anyways.
@Paul would you share any more specific or generalized goals you have in mind so we may better understand the landscape of what you may hope to achieve?
I think aiming to increase the analog IP we have is your best bet here for producing something novel.
Analog on gf180mcu is still largely unexplored compared to the crazy things people are doing in sky130 TT analog slots now
I believe there are also a lot of ways you can still make competitive products with analog, even on such an old process.

Wholeheartedly agree. 
This thought also aligns somewhat with GF's general stance when deciding to stop pushing <12nm
@Tholin can you share some ideas that are more specific? 
-# sorry my ignorance is showing

My world view when it comes to analog is pretty narrow. I know people who do anything with music production equipment (i.e. synthesizer builders) would appreciate chips implementing the highly specific filter or VCO designs they need, with some mixed-signal processing sprinkled in for good measure. I know that a lot of analog oscillator and filter integrated circuitry operating on audio frequencies is very old designs from decades ago that may not even be in production anymore.
Retro computing has a lot of mixed-signal sound and video generators that aren’t just VGA or a DSP + DAC.
I swear I had one more example on my mind, but I forgot while typing up the rest.

It seems like this project's goals may be similar to Chipalooza, just intended to be on a grander scale.  But the fact Chipalooza is also targeting this shuttle might mean some of the people with the required skills and free time to tackle these kind of problems are already busy.  And some of the building blocks that will hopefully come out of Chipalooza would probably be useful for some of these more advanced goals (if gigabit ethernet/PCIE is even possible - high speed USB might be a more achievable goal?)

@Paul if you are interested and @Tholin is willing, I would be happy to help out integrating a SoC with Tholin's voltage regulator for one of the slots if that would be of interest.  I wouldn't be able to do a self trimming oscillator as Tim suggested (though if anyone else here is available to do that I'd be happy to integrate it), but we could have something that was either driven from a ring oscillator or an external clock, with the ability to do USB CDC (traditional Full Speed only) if an external clock is supplied.  We'd use the latest version of Tholin's standard cell library to prove that works as expected in a complex project.  I haven't looked into Staf's SRAMs, but potentially we could use them as well, providing initial results from run 2 are positive.

I've recently been working on an improved version of BIO - with more predictable instruction timing and improved instruction set over Baochip's BIO (https://www.crowdsupply.com/baochip/dabao/updates/bio-the-bao-i-o-co-processor), I don't know how usable that will be by the run 3 deadline but it would be cool to have the opportunity to tape it out even if it was a bit WIP.

messages.content: Yeah, that's basically a straight port of the Baochip version, and it doesn't have a host CPU.  My aim is an improved version of BIO + either TinyQV or a more fully featured RISC-V core as the host.

@Andrew Wingate DeepAI is making it easier to gamble on open source silicon by giving out free silicon compilation to people pushing the boundaries. That's why we got the 10 slots. Our own project is developing a new ai agentic cpu architecture, and we're starting small. We just think custom silicon should be as plentiful and as easy to make as opens source code

High speed interfaces are an interest of @baragonaru, who's the lead designer of Chippy, the ai agent CPU. We're also following the guidance of @Tim 'mithro' Ansell on what projects would help open source silicon the most, along with a few advisors and friends, like in this thread
Like what was said earlier, analog work is something that is feasible and is lacking on the open source end. Projects like the voltage regulator or the calibration chip are along this line
@Tholin yes, let's do the regulator. Do you want to fit it inside the analog calibration chip? Could be interesting way of testing and getting some instrumental value out of it
@RebelMike sure, we want to do something with RISC-V this run, could you DM me with your 1 pager on the chip?

@RebelMike, @bunnie has seen you were working on BIO improvements https://discord.com/channels/1361349522684510449/1413281558407942236/1559267339713642547 and is interested in reading/seeing more if you have anything.
I should write something up 😄

I don’t think I’ve even pushed the repo to GitHub yet. But the main things I’ve done:
Use FemtoRV as the core.
2 clocks per instruction for all instructions except memory access and branches. Predictable performance in general to allow cycle counting. No C extension.
Add some B extension instructions. In particular I found rotates being missing a problem when writing for BIO as it meant you couldn’t easily shift bits out to an arbitrary pin. Bit and byte reverse. And the logical ops with one inverted operand.

One note, so far this is a rewrite. I haven’t been referencing the original BIO implementation, just the spec. But also I haven’t got as far as doing the FIFOs yet - I’ve just got GPIO working on a single core. So possibly this would be a good point to try and transplant what I have into the original BIO implementation, especially if this project might be gaining a deadline.

I guess @bunnie is somewhere that blocks discord

> Ah that's pretty nice to have the B extensions. Are these specifiable as a standard compiler option or will this require hand coded assembly?
> 
> Lol I had the theory that you would not want to cycle count because you can rtl simulate, but it's not a bad idea to shorten the pipeline regardless
> 
> The C instructions are sort of important actually for both fetch bandwidth and instruction density. 4k is very small
> 
> I was contemplating a next gen for bio, so this is useful. Actually a test bench is really valuable, I would like to copy any test code he has and add it to the tests, and maybe start a CI if there is actually interest in developing the BIO

> Not sure if he is interested in collaborative work tho or if he would prefer just to dev on a branch and then I cherry pick whatever I want for a next tape out
> 
> I would like to roughly double the performance of bio by the next gen
~ bunnie
